text: At twelve, Jesus amazed the teachers in the temple. Then He went home "and was subject to" His parents, and "increased in wisdom… and in favour."
explanation:
The boy Jesus was asking and answering questions that astonished the scholars of Jerusalem. He understood more than His parents did. Yet when Mary and Joseph found Him, "He went down with them… and was subject to them." The very next verse says He "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men."

We often think we only need to honour people who are smarter, richer or more qualified than us. God watches the heart. "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you in due time."

text: Esther asked for nothing except what the king's attendant advised, "and Esther obtained favour in the sight of all."
explanation:
Every young woman brought before King Ahasuerus could ask for anything she wanted to wear. Esther simply took the advice of Hegai, the king's attendant (not a believer, and not someone she had to listen to). Ruth likewise humbled herself, followed her mother-in-law's counsel, and gleaned in the fields, the humblest work available. That's where she found favour with Boaz.

Submission isn't weakness. Over and over in Scripture, favour flows to those who are humble and teachable. Honour the people God has placed around you, and watch Him lift you up.

text: "I also am a man under authority," said the centurion. That's why his word carried authority too.
explanation:
The Roman centurion told Jesus He didn't need to come to his house: "Only speak a word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man under authority, having soldiers under me." He understood that authority flows to those who are themselves under authority. Jesus marvelled at his faith.

Some believers think that once they're saved, they belong to the universal church and no local church. But Scripture speaks of real congregations, elders, and "not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together." There's safety, accountability and anointing in God's house. Lone rangers are easy targets.

text: "It is He who gives you power to get wealth, that He may establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers."
explanation:
God told Israel, "When your silver and your gold are multiplied": when, not if. His concern was that their hearts would be lifted up and they'd say, "My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth." Wealth isn't the problem; forgetting the Giver is. Often provision comes so naturally (a timely tip, a better job, a discount) that we miss that it's the Lord.

And the purpose of the wealth? "To establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers": Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, a covenant of grace long before the law. Sending the gospel out, feeding the hungry, caring for the young: that takes provision. God blesses you to be a blessing.

text: Melchizedek brought out bread and wine. Don't "do" Communion; receive it from His hands.
explanation:
After Abraham's victory, he was met by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who "brought out bread and wine." Jesus is "a High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." He is still the One bringing out the bread and the wine.

If you think of Communion as something you do, it can become a ritual. But if you see it as something you receive from Him (fresh bread for your body's repair, fresh wine reminding you your sins are forgiven), it never gets old. Ask yourself, "Have I received Communion today?"

text: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain." From one verse about oxen, Paul drew a New Testament truth.
explanation:
"Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or does He say it altogether for our sakes?" Paul saw in an obscure law about farm animals a picture of those who labour to thresh out the grain of God's Word for others. Let them share in the harvest. Yet Paul himself chose not to use that right, "lest we hinder the gospel of Christ."

That's how to read the Old Testament: it isn't discarded, it's fulfilled. The New tells you what; the Old often shows you how, and above all it unveils Christ. Don't close half your Bible because you've found grace.

text: "He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much." God calls money the least, and souls the true riches.
explanation:
"If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?" Money, in God's eyes, is the smallest thing He entrusts to us, and it isn't clean by default. How we handle it shows whether He can trust us with what matters far more: people, influence, gifts.

Jesus said, "Give alms of such things as you have; then indeed all things are clean to you." Giving sanctifies the rest. It's not about earning God's love, which is already yours. It's honouring Him as the source, with a heart that's grateful rather than grasping.
